extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of journalism, media studies, and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Describes and explains the informal 'Dover test' — using public reaction to returning war casualties (as shown in the media) as an indicator of whether the U.S. population supports continued military action. Covers interpretation, limitations, and historical/media-policy impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dover test (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An informal journalistic phrase: assess whether the general U.S. population supports U.S. participation in a war or military action by observing public reaction to returning war casualties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test looks specifically at reactions to the sight of casualties returning (e.g., flag-draped caskets arriving at Dover Air Force Base) as presented in news coverage. It is explicitly informal and functions as a heuristic rather than a formal measurement tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passing vs. failing interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the U.S. population continues to support the war after news coverage of returning casualties, the government is said to have 'passed' the Dover test; if public support falls, the government has 'failed' the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation is a binary heuristic: 'continued support' implies passing and likely continued warfare without a reduction in government popularity; 'loss of support' implies failing and potential decline in popularity. The article notes this is a commonly used framing rather than a precise metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-coverage as an intervening factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether images or reports of returning casualties are shown in the media directly affects the operation of the Dover test (i.e., people cannot react to what they do not see).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments or administrations have sometimes restricted media coverage of returning casualties (e.g., bans on showing deceased returning to Dover) specifically to avoid subjecting public opinion to the Dover test. Thus media access/visibility is a key practical condition for the test to operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informality, partisan use, and interpretive flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dover test is not a formal scientific test; its results are hard to measure objectively and are often invoked to support partisan positions rather than to determine actual public support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different factions may use reactions to further their own motives; the article emphasizes that the test is 'used more often to support someone's opinion or to question government actions than to actually determine the level of public support for the war.' Treat conclusions drawn from the Dover test as politically contested and not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Application and impact of the Dover test has varied historically (e.g., Vietnam, Panama, Somalia, first Gulf War, Iraq/Afghanistan) depending on the conflict, media practices, and policy decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate how the visibility of casualties and the public reaction affected policy decisions (e.g., withdrawal after Mogadishu) and how administrations have attempted to manage coverage. Use historical context when invoking the test — outcomes depend on era-specific media norms and rules on coverage.
